source: Vitello and Salvi (2023) Gestalt's Perspective on Insight: A Recap Based on Recent Behavioral and Neuroscientific Evidence
finding: Gestalt view: insight is productive thinking. The solver restructures the problem's elements and the answer arrives as a sudden whole (off-on), like flipping a bistable figure. Opposed to Thorndike's reproductive trial and error. Kohler's 1925 chimpanzee that saw crates as building blocks is the founding animal case.
numbers: Review, no new N. Cites Kohler 1925, Wertheimer 1959, Maier 1940, Koffka 1935.
limits: Authors are Neo-Gestalt and read past work generously. Founding studies are described, not re-run.
agent_relevance: Treat restructuring as a named operator: drop the current framing and re-describe the elements, not only search harder inside the old frame.

source: Metcalfe (1986) feeling-of-warmth ratings, as reported in Vitello and Salvi (2023)
finding: Solvers rated how close they were to the answer. On insight problems warmth stayed flat and jumped only in the last 10 s before the solution. On analytic problems warmth rose gradually. Answers after sudden jumps were more often correct than answers after gradual rises.
numbers: Last 10 s window for insight problems. N not given in the secondary source.
limits: Primary (and Metcalfe and Wiebe 1987) not opened; numbers come from the review. Later work (Durso 1994, Novick and Sherman 2003, Cushen and Wiley 2012) found incremental patterns as well.
agent_relevance: Mid-run self-assessed progress will look flat before a restructure, so a progress monitor must not read 'no progress' as 'no hidden progress'.

source: Durso et al. (1994) word-pair relatedness during a riddle, as reported in Graf et al. (2023)
finding: Solvers repeatedly rated how related word pairs were. Solution-relevant pairs were rated as more similar the nearer people got to the solution. Authors: a long fuse warns of the impending reorganisation.
numbers: No N in the secondary source.
quote: Like dynamite, the insightful solution explodes on the solver's cognitive landscape with breathtaking suddenness, but ... a long fuse warns
limits: Found only incremental patterns. Primary not opened.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to pure suddenness: hidden gradual build-up exists, so an agent can probe element-to-goal relatedness before the flip.

source: Novick and Sherman (2003) Exp. 2 anagram solvability judgments, as reported in Graf et al. (2023)
finding: Within 250 ms of anagram offset people could not solve, but got better at telling solvable from unsolvable anagrams as presentation time grew. Read as gradual accumulation of solution-relevant information.
numbers: 250 ms window after stimulus offset. N not in secondary source.
limits: Primary not opened. Also found sudden patterns in some trials. Verbal anagrams, not spatial restructuring.
agent_relevance: Partial information exists before the answer; a cheap solvability check could be a signal for when to switch frames.

source: Ohlsson (1992) Information-processing explanations of insight and related phenomena, as quoted in Graf et al. (2023) and Oellinger et al. (2017)
finding: Representational change theory (RCT): an impasse comes from a wrong initial representation. It is broken by constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition and re-encoding, driven by spreading activation from working memory. Ohlsson also said the sudden appearance of the full solution may be an illusion of poor introspective access.
numbers: Theory paper, no N.
quote: the sudden appearance of the complete solution in consciousness is an illusion caused by our lack of introspective access
limits: Primary not opened. Developed on matchstick and nine-dot tasks; generality to open-ended problems is untested.
agent_relevance: Direct match to the schema: impasse state then a restructuring operator. The illusion point means suddenness may be an unlogged-step artefact, which an agent trace can check.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider and Rhenius (1999) matchstick arithmetic: constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition, as reported in Graf et al. (2023) and Oellinger et al. (2017)
finding: Matchstick equations fixed by moving one stick. Problems that need loosening a strong constraint (take a stick from an operator, not a number) or breaking a tight perceptual chunk are harder. This is the core RCT test.
numbers: No figures in the secondary sources.
limits: Primary not opened. Tests difficulty, not temporal dynamics.
agent_relevance: Difficulty tracks how tightly the representation is held; tight chunks need explicit decomposition prompts.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson and Raney (2001) eye movements on matchstick problems, as reported in Graf et al. (2023)
finding: Solvers and non-solvers both looked mostly at the numbers first. Only in the final third of the time did later solvers shift gaze to the operators (the plus sign). Non-solvers stayed on the numbers.
numbers: Final third of solving time; about five minutes per problem. N not in secondary source.
limits: Cannot say whether the shift was sudden because the last third may last minutes. Same pattern in Tseng et al. 2014. Primary not opened.
agent_relevance: A stuck frame can be read from where attention goes; for an LLM, look at which parts of the problem the reasoning keeps naming.

source: Graf, Danek, Vaci and Bilalic (2023) Tracing Cognitive Processes in Insight Problem Solving: Using GAMs and Change Point Analysis to Uncover Restructuring
finding: Re-analysis of eye tracking on a constraint-relaxation matchstick problem in 10 time bins. Solvers' dwell on the critical plus sign bursts up just before the solution. ANOVA and polynomial terms smear this into a gradual rise. GAMs and change points find the abrupt shift. After an explicit hint the eventual solvers shift gradually instead.
numbers: Only 34% solved in the first 5 min; the hint added 11%. 10 bins of 10% of solving time. Non-solvers showed an immediate burst after the hint that then faded.
quote: only nonlinear statistical models ... correctly identified the abrupt representational change
limits: One task, re-analysed data from Bilalic et al. 2019. Change-point models need the number of change points set in advance. Hinted runs are a different process.
agent_relevance: Restructuring is sudden at the level of attention, and 'gradual' findings can be statistical artefacts. To test suddenness in agent logs use change-point models, not linear trends.

source: Danek and Wiley (2017) What about False Insights? Deconstructing the Aha! Experience Along Its Multiple Dimensions
finding: Aha can accompany wrong answers (false insights). Aha has three core parts: Pleasure, Suddenness, Certainty. Correct solutions were faster and had stronger Aha, Pleasure, Suddenness and Certainty. Relief marked correct, Surprise marked incorrect.
numbers: 70 participants, 35 magic tricks, 2450 trials; 1778 solved: 36.8% correct (654), 63.2% wrong (1124). Aha mean 66.50 (SD 18.42) correct vs 52.34 (SD 18.78) wrong, t(69)=10.21. Time 35.81 s vs 42.46 s. 37% (417 of 1124) of wrong answers had Aha above the mean for correct ones.
limits: Magic-trick stimuli, not classic restructuring puzzles. Self-report only. Published online 2016 (Front Psychol).
agent_relevance: A sudden, certain flip is not proof of a correct answer. Never use felt insight as a stop signal; verify.

source: Salvi, Bricolo, Kounios, Bowden and Beeman (2016) Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions, as reported in Vitello and Salvi (2023)
finding: Self-reported insight solutions were correct more often than analytic ones across compound remote associates, anagrams, rebus puzzles and line drawings. Insight solvers time out more than they err, because they have no partial answer to guess.
numbers: No N in the secondary source. Replicated on magic tricks by Danek 2014 and Hedne 2016, and by Laukkonen 2021.
limits: Primary not opened. The accuracy edge may reflect that hard answers are only reported when the solver is sure.
agent_relevance: Insight-mode answers are accurate but come with no intermediate product; add an analytic fallback that produces partial guesses.

source: Salvi et al. (2020) pupil dilation before Aha, as reported in Vitello and Salvi (2023)
finding: Pupil size rose before people announced an insight, peaking about 200 ms before the report, as in bistable-figure switches. It did so for wrong insights too. Replicated by Becker et al. 2021.
numbers: 60.5% likelihood of a pupil increase in insight trials (as quoted by the review); a 560 ms window of right-temporal gamma plus pupil change before insight reports.
limits: Primary not opened. A pupil change is a marker, not proof of when the answer reached awareness. Locus coeruleus link is speculative.
agent_relevance: Physiological support for a discrete reset event; no direct use for an LLM beyond the idea of a reset.

source: Laukkonen and Tangen (2017) Necker cube priming and Bianchi et al. (2020) think in opposites, as reported in Vitello and Salvi (2023)
finding: Watching a bistable Necker cube (vs two alternating cubes) led to more insight on later verbal problems. Prompting people to think in opposites on visuospatial problems produced more insight than an overt hint, by widening the search space.
numbers: No N in the secondary source.
limits: Primary not opened. Priming effects are often fragile.
agent_relevance: An inversion prompt (read the task the opposite way) is a cheap restructuring operator for the agent.

source: Laukkonen et al. (2021) dynamometer measure of Aha, as reported in Vitello and Salvi (2023)
finding: People squeezed a dynamometer harder, in a single slope, during Aha, and squeeze magnitude matched solution accuracy.
numbers: No N in the secondary source.
limits: Primary not opened. Same lab links Aha to prediction-error updating (Laukkonen et al. 2023).
agent_relevance: Felt strength tracks correctness on average but is no guarantee.

source: Korovkin et al. (2021) ten-penny problem, symmetric vs asymmetric solutions, as reported in Vitello and Salvi (2023)
finding: Same problem, two valid solution types. The symmetric (holistic) solution got higher Aha and elegance ratings than the asymmetric one. So Aha depends on the solution found, not the problem.
numbers: No N in the secondary source.
limits: Primary not opened. One problem.
agent_relevance: Elegance feels right but proves nothing; use it only as a tie-break after verification.

source: Oellinger, Fedor, Brodt and Szathmary (2017) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization
finding: Relaxing constraints is necessary but not sufficient. Solving needs both a relaxed constraint and an efficient search criterion (maximization). Hints to relax constraints alone barely helped. Adding the maximization hint lifted solving to 72%.
numbers: N = 4 x 30 (119 analysed). Solved: control 3/30 (10%), line hint 2/29 (7%), intersection hint 6/28 (21%), maximization hint 21/29 (72%). Max vs control chi2(1,59)=23.80, p<.0001, phi=.64. Hint given at 5 min.
limits: One multi-step problem; hint timing fixed.
agent_relevance: A restructuring operator alone is not enough. Pair it with a search criterion and a progress test, as the schema pairs operators with states and guardrails.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod and Chronicle (2001) nine-dot model: maximization plus progress monitoring, as described in Oellinger et al. (2017)
finding: Computational account in the nothing-special tradition. Each move connects as many dots as possible (maximization). A look-ahead check of remaining lines vs unconnected dots (progress monitoring) flags failure and sends search outside the grid. Look-ahead 2 flags failure earlier than look-ahead 1.
numbers: No N here.
limits: Primary not opened. Ohlsson's reply: search heuristics do not explain where a new search space comes from. Weaker where no obvious progress metric exists.
agent_relevance: A formal trigger for restructuring: a failed progress test fires the restructuring operator.

source: Kaplan and Simon (1990) In search of insight, as described in Oellinger et al. (2017)
finding: Nothing-special view: insight problems are ordinary search with huge or ill-defined spaces. Making crucial features more salient shrinks the space. Shown on the mutilated checkerboard where more salient cues raised solution rates.
numbers: No N in the secondary source.
limits: Primary not opened. Competes with the special-process Gestalt and RCT view.
agent_relevance: The cheap fix may be better search control and feature salience, not a special flip.

source: Weisberg and Alba (1981), Scheerer (1963), Lung and Dominowski (1985): hints about the source of difficulty, as summarised in Oellinger et al. (2017)
finding: Equating insight with relaxing one source of difficulty is misleading. Telling people the key, directly or via transfer tasks, does not reliably raise solution rates on the nine-dot problem.
numbers: No figures in the secondary source.
limits: Primary not opened. Replicated by Kershaw 2013 and Oellinger, Jones and Knoblich 2014 per the same text.
agent_relevance: A restructuring prompt alone will not unstick an agent; add search guidance and checking.

source: Oellinger, Szathmary and Fedor (2023) Search and insight processes in card sorting games
finding: A card sorting game with hidden, non-obvious rules elicits Aha and restructuring-like behaviour. The further the hidden rule is from prior knowledge, the harder it is. People use different strategies on the same problem (feature integration or deliberate testing).
numbers: Two online experiments, N = 546 in total.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; result tables not examined. Includes a cognitive model sketch merging search and representational change.
agent_relevance: Rule discovery with prior-knowledge traps resembles ARC-style puzzles.

source: Wiley and Miller (2026) Aha! Ratings as Metacognitive Judgments
finding: Aha is better seen as a Judgment of Aha (JOA), inferred from cues, not a direct readout of restructuring. JOAs were highest when the solver made a correct first move, not when an initial representation had to be revised.
numbers: 377 students, 4 object-move puzzles, 1508 trials, 1164 analysed. Correct > wrong JOA, F(1,1091)=112.17, p<.001; partial R2=.09 (95% CI .06 to .12), f2=.099. Growth mindset strengthened the link for initially correct solutions.
limits: Spatial puzzles, 180 s limit, student sample.
agent_relevance: Aha-like confidence is a correctness cue, not a restructuring cue. Do not take a feeling of insight as proof the agent changed frame.

source: Macchi, Turco, Inglese and Caravona (2026) The Eyes as a Mirror of the Unconscious: pupil dilation and unconscious analytic thought in insight
finding: Unconscious analytic thought view: restructuring during incubation is high-level unconscious work. Solvers kept high, constant pupil dilation during an arithmetic distractor phase. Non-solvers and controls showed falling dilation.
numbers: Group (solver, non-solver, control) x time interaction significant on pupil size. EyeLink 1000 Plus, 1000 Hz downsampled to 100 Hz. N not captured in my read.
limits: Only abstract and preprocessing read in detail. Pupil effort is an indirect measure; incubation effects are replication-weak (see parent field notes).
agent_relevance: Supports a background pass between attempts instead of one pass, but treat as weak.

source: Doulfoukar, Pezzulo and Stuyck (2026) Unveiling the Aha! moment: a computational account of insight in active inference
finding: Insight modelled as Bayesian model reduction (BMR) in a modified Wisconsin Card Sorting Task. The model shows discontinuous jumps in behaviour and confidence, a transient peak in Bayesian surprise and a phasic rise in expected precision. Impasse is a transient state of high uncertainty over actions. Offline generative replay proposes alternative models for reduction.
numbers: Agent without BMR: uncertainty peaks near trial 25, rule inferred at trial 33, fully certain by trial 35. Learning rate eta = 0.5 set low on purpose to match human delay (Oellinger 2023).
limits: Simulation only, one task; discontinuity is built in and not tested against rival models in the part read.
agent_relevance: A formal template for our S/O design: impasse state, then a model-reduction or replay step that prunes framings. Links to the replay subfields.

source: Orru, Piarulli, Conversano and Gemignani (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT (9 Jan 2023 version) tried 30 verbal insight problems from Ansburg and Dominowski (2000). Its total matched the most probable score of a 20-person human sample on practice, transfer and pooled sets. It fell for the trap on the first pear-tree/plums problem and answered 144.
numbers: Practice 7/15, transfer 5/15; difference Fisher exact p<.72. Human solution rate 0.55 (practice) and 0.35 (transfer), n = 20. ChatGPT inside the top 5% most probable human outcomes on practice and pooled sets.
limits: One run, one model. Control and strategic instructions plus per-item feedback were given after errors, so not zero-shot. Not a replication. 1990s items may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that models fall for the same obvious-reading traps and gain from strategic instructions; human-parity claim is weak.

source: Qiu, Zhou and Schooler (2026) The Cost of Coordination: Why Multi-Agent LLMs Explore More But Discover Less (preprint)
finding: ChatGPT-4o agents solved situation puzzles (lateral thinking) solo or as two-agent teams. Teams were less accurate despite asking across broader question categories. Mediation: 47% protocol failure (discussion cut host-directed questions) and 53% residual coordination cost in convergent integration.
numbers: N = 82 in a 2 (solo vs team) x 2 (time) design. Doubling time raised question volume equally and kept the team to solo ratio.
limits: Abstract only seen. Preprint, not peer reviewed. One model.
agent_relevance: Unstructured multi-agent chat helps divergence and hurts convergence on the restructured answer. Supports one agent with a scaffold over a free-talking crowd.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reports an aha moment in an intermediate DeepSeek-R1-Zero checkpoint. Mid-solution the model writes that it has an aha moment and re-evaluates. Operationalised as a sudden rise in the word wait during reflection over RL training.
numbers: Evidence is one transcript (Table 2) and a rise in wait frequency (Figure 9b). No accuracy numbers for the aha step in the passage read.
quote: Wait, wait. Wait. That's an aha moment I can flag here.
limits: Lexical marker, not a measured representational change. No control for base-model behaviour.
agent_relevance: Reflective re-evaluation is trainable by outcome reward, but the insight label is borrowed without a restructuring test.

source: Liu, Chen, Li, Qi, Pang, Du, Lee and Lin (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (COLM 2025)
finding: Failed replication of the claim that RL creates the aha moment. DeepSeek-V3-Base already produces self-reflection keywords (Aha, wait) before RL. In R1-Zero self-reflection is more frequent but not positively correlated with accuracy.
numbers: 500 MATH questions, DeepSeek-V3-Base-685B self-hosted, 8 responses per question. Also finds GRPO length bias that inflates wrong-answer length (fix: Dr. GRPO).
limits: Keyword detection for reflection; MATH only. Earlier open replicas (Liu 2025b; Yeo et al. 2025) agreed.
agent_relevance: LLM aha is mostly pre-existing behaviour. Counting wait tokens is not evidence of restructuring.

source: Zhou, Li et al. (2025) R1-Zero's Aha Moment in Visual Reasoning on a 2B Non-SFT Model
finding: Claims first multimodal replication of the aha moment: RL on Qwen2-VL-2B base (no SFT) shows self-reflection and growing response length.
numbers: CVBench accuracy 59.47%, about +30 points over the base model and about +2 over the SFT model.
limits: Aha judged from examples and length growth; Liu et al. 2025 suggest reflection may be latent in base models.
agent_relevance: Reflection can emerge cheaply under RL; no isolation of representational change.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma and Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Benchmark of lateral-thinking multiple-choice puzzles that need breaking default commonsense associations. Closest LLM test of leaving the default frame. Pointer only.
numbers: PDF text extraction returned empty; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Take numbers from a later read.
agent_relevance: The project's own BRAINTEASER item set is a restructuring test bed.
